title: Intensive Math Instruction and Educational Attainment: Long-Run Impacts of Double-Dose Algebra
research_question: What are the long-run effects of intensive, doubled instructional time in 9th grade algebra—combined with altered peer composition and a problem-solving curriculum—on students' course performance, math achievement, high school graduation, and college enrollment? How do these effects vary by students' underlying reading skills, and do test-score gains accurately predict longer-run educational attainment gains?
data_description: The study uses longitudinal administrative data from Chicago Public Schools (CPS) tracking students from 8th grade through college enrollment. Variables include demographics (gender, race/ethnicity, free/reduced-price lunch status, special education status, Census block-group poverty and SES measures), 8th grade Iowa Tests of Basic Skills (ITBS) math and reading percentile scores, detailed high school transcripts (course-by-course grades, credits, subject), standardized test scores (PLAN exams in fall of 10th and 11th grade; ACT in April of 11th grade), high school graduation within four and five years, and college enrollment data matched from the National Student Clearinghouse. The analytic sample consists of first-time 9th graders entering CPS in fall 2003 and fall 2004, restricted to 73 high schools with at least one double-dose classroom and excluding selective magnet, alternative, and special education schools. The unit of observation is the student.
institutional_context: Chicago Public Schools, facing high 9th grade course failure rates—especially in algebra—following its late-1990s adoption of a college-prep curriculum, introduced a policy beginning fall 2003 requiring all entering 9th graders who scored below the national median on the 8th grade ITBS math exam to enroll in two periods of algebra rather than one. Eligible students took a regular full-year algebra class plus a full-year algebra support class, receiving 90 minutes of daily math instruction. CPS provided specific curricula (Agile Mind, Cognitive Tutor), lesson plans, and professional development emphasizing problem-solving, verbal exposition of mathematical concepts, and small-group work. Schools were advised to schedule both periods consecutively, with the same teacher, and with the same classmates, increasing tracking by skill. Compliance with the assignment rule was strong in the first two cohorts (2003 and 2004) but eroded thereafter; the test-score-based rule generated sharp variation in treatment around the 50th percentile threshold.
